proposedDescription: Greater celandine brings small yellow flowers to shady edges, gardens, and disturbed woodland. This leafy herb lives for more than one season or behaves as a biennial, spreading readily by seed where conditions suit it. Its deeply divided leaves and orange-yellow sap help separate it from other yellow-flowered plants. Originally from Eurasia, it has become established beyond its native range. The sap can irritate skin, so this is a plant to recognize without breaking its stems by hand.
identification: Look for clusters of four-petaled yellow flowers, lobed leaves, and long, slender seed capsules. Do not deliberately expose skin to the sap.
actions: Wear gloves when removing small unwanted plants, and work before they set seed. Recheck the area for seedlings.
researchNotes: Synthesized morphology and garden behavior with Kew's range and life-form account. Kept greater celandine distinct from lesser celandine; no unsupported nationwide impact claim.

sources.title: Kew Plants of the World Online: Chelidonium majus

claims: Yellow four-petaled flowers; divided leaves; irritating colored sap; rapid reseeding.
Accepted Eurasian herb with introduced populations outside its native range.

proposedDescription: This cellar spider belongs to the long-legged spiders that hang beneath loose webs in sheltered corners. Pholcus manueli has been recorded in cellars and other buildings, including a garage from which it was first described. Although its name was established from American specimens, the World Spider Catalog treats it as an Asian species introduced to the United States. Several cellar spiders look similar, so a web in a basement is a useful clue, not enough to identify this particular species.
identification: Long, thin legs and an inverted position in an irregular web suggest a cellar spider. Species-level identification needs an expert examination.
actions: Photograph the spider and its web if documenting a sighting. Seek identification before treating a familiar house spider as this species.
researchNotes: USDA field observations independently support building habitat; Bern's catalog resolves accepted identity and introduced status. Family traits are presented as family traits, not unique diagnostic characters.

sources.title: USDA Forest Service: Spiders of Milbridge, Maine

claims: Pholcid web and leg traits; P. manueli collected in a cellar and government building.
Accepted species with Asian distribution and introduced United States status.

proposedDescription: Centipedegrass is the pale-green, low-growing lawn grass often planted in warm parts of the country. It creeps across the soil on aboveground runners, gradually forming a coarse-textured turf rather than an upright clump. Its leaves alternate along the runners, giving them the appearance that inspired its common name. This grass is adapted to acidic, relatively low-fertility soils. Because it is widely cultivated, a patch beside a lawn should be described in that context rather than automatically labeled a harmful invasion.
identification: Look for light-green blades alternating along creeping runners and a slender, single seed spike. St. Augustinegrass has opposite leaves.
actions: Keep planted turf within its intended area. For unwanted patches, confirm the grass before selecting a removal method with local extension advice.
researchNotes: Both university accounts support identification and turf ecology. Deliberately avoided equating cultivation or escape with demonstrated ecological damage.

sources.title: UF/IFAS: Identification of Common Florida Lawn Grasses

claims: Warm-season turf; aboveground stolons; alternate leaves; acid low-fertility soils.
Centipedegrass blade, sheath, growth-habit and seedhead characteristics.

proposedDescription: Centipede tongavine is a tropical climbing plant whose leaves change dramatically as it grows. Young shoots creep or climb with relatively simple leaves; older shoots supported by a tree or another surface can produce much larger, deeply divided leaves. Aerial roots help the vine hold on as it climbs. Native across parts of Asia and the Pacific, it is grown ornamentally beyond that range. Its changing leaf shape makes identifying mature and juvenile plants together especially useful.
identification: Compare young and mature leaves and look for clasping aerial roots. Deeply divided mature leaves differ from the simpler juvenile foliage.
actions: Keep cultivated vines contained and do not discard living cuttings in natural areas. Photograph several growth stages for identification.
researchNotes: Kew and NParks support identity, life form and morphology. Excluded the older GISD account of E. pinnatum cv. Aureum to avoid transferring golden-pothos impacts to this species.

sources.title: Kew Plants of the World Online: Epipremnum pinnatum

claims: Root-climbing habit and contrasting juvenile and mature foliage.
Accepted tropical climber with Asian-Pacific native range and introduced records.

proposedDescription: This microscopic diatom is known from freshwater plankton and is associated with the smaller freshwater forms of Actinocyclus normanii. Viewed through a microscope, its round silica shell has a patterned surface of pores that specialists use for identification. Its history in the Great Lakes is less straightforward than an introduction date might suggest: older sediment evidence has raised questions about whether it arrived recently at all. Even the boundary between named forms is uncertain, making careful identification more useful than a simple invasive label.
identification: Identification requires microscopy of the circular valve, pore arrangement, and specialized structures. Small size alone does not securely identify the named form.
actions: Have a qualified diatom specialist examine samples. Record sampling details; do not attempt species-specific treatment based on water appearance.
researchNotes: Research gap: queue spelling f. subsala differs from f. subsalsa in the reviewed accounts, and Diatoms.org questions a clear boundary between forms. Keep ID unchanged pending taxonomic reconciliation; native status remains uncertain.

sources.title: Diatoms of North America: Actinocyclus normanii
USGS Great Lakes account: Actinocyclus normanii f. subsalsa

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Diatoms of North America editorial team
claims: Circular pore-patterned valves; small freshwater form; uncertainty in form separation.
Freshwater plankton ecology and uncertainty over introduction history from sediment evidence.

proposedDescription: Skeletonema potamos is a tiny diatom that drifts in fresh and slightly brackish water, often as short chains of cells. Its delicate silica walls are so small that it can be overlooked even under a light microscope. Researchers studying the Danube found that it became a larger part of the river's plankton community as water temperatures rose. Its original range remains uncertain, and finding it in a water sample does not by itself establish a harmful bloom or a recent introduction.
identification: Specialists look for very small cylindrical cells joined in chains by marginal structures. Reliable identification may require detailed microscopy.
actions: Document the waterbody and sampling conditions and seek specialist confirmation. Avoid transporting untreated water or wet equipment between waterbodies.
researchNotes: Combined USGS ecological context with the independent Danube study's original morphology and long-term observations. The warming relationship is regional and correlational, not a universal impact claim.

sources.title: USGS Great Lakes account: Skeletonema potamos
Duleba and colleagues: Skeletonema potamos in the River Danube

claims: Small chain-forming diatom in freshwater and brackish habitats; uncertain original range.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Duleba et al. Danube research team
claims: Original cell morphology; increasing relative abundance correlated with warming during 1979–2012.

proposedDescription: Cereal cyst nematode is a microscopic roundworm that feeds inside the roots of wheat, barley, oats, and other grasses. Damaged roots have more difficulty supplying the plant with water and nutrients, which can leave uneven patches of weak or stunted crop. After a female dies, her hardened body becomes a cyst that shelters eggs in the soil. Those persistent cysts make the problem longer-lived than one growing season, while the symptoms above ground can easily be mistaken for other crop stresses.
identification: Stunting and poor patches are warning signs, not a diagnosis. Root and soil samples need laboratory examination to distinguish related cyst nematodes.
actions: Ask an agricultural diagnostic service how to sample affected patches. Use confirmed species identity to guide crop rotation and resistant-variety choices.
researchNotes: UC Davis biology and Oregon State's regional management synthesis independently support the draft. H. filipjevi is a distinct look-alike; resistance and diagnosis should not be generalized across species.

sources.title: Oregon State Extension: Cereal Cyst Nematodes

claims: Cereal root parasite; life cycle and persistent egg-bearing cysts.
Root damage and nonspecific crop symptoms; species diagnosis informs rotations and resistance.

proposedDescription: The cereal leaf beetle is a small insect with metallic blue wing covers and an orange-red area behind its head. Its larvae are easier to notice by what they leave behind: narrow strips of damaged tissue on cereal and grass leaves. A dark coating of their own waste often hides the larvae's pale bodies. Heavy feeding can reduce the leaf area a grain crop needs to fill its seeds, but natural enemies also help keep populations in check, making field monitoring important.
identification: Look for blue-winged, orange-thoraxed adults and waste-coated larvae feeding along leaves. Similar Oulema beetles may need expert separation.
actions: Inspect crop leaves and consult local extension thresholds before treatment. Preserve beneficial insects rather than spraying automatically after a single sighting.
researchNotes: USU supports feeding, life cycle and crop management; the UK recording scheme independently supports adult morphology and look-alike limitations. Avoided assigning all striped leaf damage to this species.

sources.title: Utah State University Extension: Cereal Leaf Beetle

claims: Adult and larval appearance; leaf injury; monitoring and natural enemies.
Adult size and coloration; close similarity to O. rufocyanea.

proposedDescription: Cereal rye is an upright annual grass grown for grain, forage, and soil cover. Its tall stems carry dense, bristly seed heads that may lean as they mature, while a network of roots helps hold the soil. It is a familiar agricultural plant that can also appear outside the places where it was sown. Despite the similar name, cereal rye is not the same as the ryegrasses used in many lawns and pastures. Identifying the seed head helps tell those grasses apart.
identification: Look for a dense, elongated grain head with conspicuous awns and flat leaves. Confirm the whole plant rather than relying on the name rye.
actions: Where rye is unwanted, document whether it is planted or growing independently. Ask local extension about preventing further seed production.
researchNotes: Two university accounts support crop uses, growth form and identification. No unsupported ecosystem-damage claim was inferred from its presence in the editorial queue.

claims: Annual grain, forage and cover crop; root and growth characteristics.
Erect grass with long-awned, dense seed spikes and flat leaves.

proposedDescription: Cerulean flaxlily forms clumps of long, sword-shaped leaves, with small pale flowers followed by glossy blue berries. Although its foliage may look grasslike at first glance, it spreads from underground rhizomes and carries its flowers on branching stalks above the leaves. Birds can disperse its fruit. Native across parts of the Old World tropics, it has also been grown as an ornamental. In Florida, UF/IFAS assesses it as invasive, so its attractive appearance should not be the only consideration when choosing a landscape plant.
identification: Look for leaves arranged in two ranks, pale flowers with prominent yellow-orange anthers, and shiny blue berries.
actions: In Florida, follow UF/IFAS advice against its use. Elsewhere, check local guidance before planting and prevent unwanted fruit or rhizome spread.
researchNotes: NParks supports morphology and dispersal; UF/IFAS supplies a separate Florida risk assessment. The Florida conclusion is explicitly regional, not a nationwide legal claim.

claims: Rhizomatous clumps; swordlike foliage; blue berries and bird dispersal.
Completed Florida assessment classifies the plant as Invasive (No Uses).

proposedDescription: Cucumber green mottle mosaic virus affects crops in the cucumber family, including cucumbers, melons, pumpkins, and squash. Infected plants may develop mottled or distorted leaves, poor growth, or damaged fruit, although symptoms vary with the crop and conditions. The virus travels with contaminated seed and plant material and can also move on hands, tools, and other surfaces. That combination makes clean planting material and careful hygiene especially important in gardens, greenhouses, and farms where susceptible crops are grown.
identification: Mosaic-patterned leaves and abnormal fruit can suggest a virus, but laboratory testing is needed to distinguish CGMMV from other problems.
actions: Pause movement of suspect plants and contact a plant diagnostic laboratory or extension service. Follow their sampling and disinfection instructions.
researchNotes: APHIS and Agriculture Victoria support hosts, symptoms and transmission. Kept Australian legal/reporting requirements out of US guidance and distinguished suspicion from a confirmed diagnosis.

sources.title: USDA APHIS: Cucumber Green Mottle Mosaic Virus
Agriculture Victoria: Cucumber green mottle mosaic virus

claims: CGMMV affects cucurbit crops and can cause serious crop damage.
Variable symptoms; contaminated seed, material and contact transmission; testing and hygiene.

proposedDescription: Chamberbitter is a small warm-season annual that can appear among garden plants, in lawns, and in other disturbed ground. Its neat rows of little leaves make a branch look like a miniature mimosa leaf, but those are individual leaves rather than leaflets. Turn a branch over and the round seed capsules underneath become a useful clue. Plants can make seed while still quite small, which is why repeatedly mowing the tops may leave the next generation ready to grow.
identification: Look beneath the leafy branches for small, rounded capsules on very short stalks. Long-stalked capsules suggest a different Phyllanthus.
actions: Pull small plants before seeds mature and use suitable mulch in beds. Mowing alone may not prevent seed production.
researchNotes: NC State botanical characters resolve the misleading compound-leaf appearance; UF/IFAS contributes independent garden-management guidance. Kept P. tenellus distinct.

claims: Two-ranked simple leaves and short-stalked capsules distinguish chamberbitter.
Warm-season annual; seeds while small; hand removal and mulch; mowing limitations.

proposedDescription: Chameleon plant is a spreading perennial with heart-shaped leaves and a strong scent when its foliage is crushed. Garden forms may have brightly patterned leaves, but the plant can also be plain green. What look like four white petals surround a short spike of tiny flowers. It thrives in moist ground and spreads through creeping underground stems, which can carry it well beyond a garden bed. Those hidden stems also make an established patch more persistent than its soft leaves might suggest.
identification: Look for heart-shaped leaves and a short flower spike surrounded by four white bracts. Leaf coloration varies among garden forms.
actions: Avoid planting it beside natural wetlands. Where removing a patch, collect creeping stems carefully and monitor for regrowth rather than only clipping leaves.
researchNotes: NC State and RHS independently support moist-site growth, spreading habit and flower structure. White structures are bracts; no nationwide invasive designation asserted.

claims: Heart-shaped foliage; scented leaves; white bracts; aggressive rhizome spread.
Spreading perennial suited to moist or boggy ground; flowers and foliage.

proposedDescription: Chandelier plant is a succulent with narrow, mottled leaves and clusters of hanging orange-red flowers. Tiny plantlets develop at the leaf tips, detach, and become new plants, helping explain its other name, mother of millions. This Madagascar native has been grown ornamentally and can establish in warm, open habitats beyond gardens. Its ability to reproduce from small pieces makes garden waste an important concern. The plant is poisonous to livestock and pets, so identification matters around grazing land and homes.
identification: Look for slender, grooved leaves with a few teeth and plantlets near their tips. Related mother-of-millions hybrids have broader leaves.
actions: Keep animals away from the plant and collect fallen plantlets when removing it. Follow local disposal guidance; do not dump living material outdoors.
researchNotes: NC State morphology and NSW field guidance agree on plantlets, toxicity and spread. Kept the broader-leaved hybrid separate and omitted Southern Hemisphere flowering dates.

claims: Madagascar succulent; narrow leaves, terminal plantlets and pendant flowers; toxicity.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: New South Wales Department of Primary Industries
claims: Plantlet and fragment spread; livestock risk; identification from related hybrid.

proposedDescription: Changing forget-me-not earns its name as its tiny flowers age from pale yellow or cream to blue. Several colors can appear on the same curling flower cluster, a helpful detail when this small plant blends into grassy ground. It is a hairy annual with slender stems and narrow leaves, originally from Europe and now established elsewhere. Roadsides, ditches, open pasture, and other disturbed places can provide suitable habitat. A close view of the flowers is much more useful for identification than a distant patch of blue.
identification: Look for different flower colors on one cluster, small five-lobed corollas, and hooked hairs on the calyx. A hand lens helps.
actions: Photograph fresh and older flowers together. Confirm identification before removing forget-me-nots, since a common name can cover several species.
researchNotes: Independent New Zealand and British Columbia floras agree on color change and morphology. No unsupported claim of severe ecological harm was added.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Myosotis discolor

claims: Annual hairy herb; cream or yellow corollas become blue; open pasture habitat.
European introduction; disturbed moist sites; flower, leaf and calyx characters.

proposedDescription: The channeled apple snail is a large freshwater snail that grazes on aquatic plants and can damage crops grown in wet fields. Its rounded shell has deep grooves between the coils, while conspicuous pink egg masses are laid above the waterline. Originally South American, it has been moved to other regions through human activity. In Hawaii, it became a serious pest of wetland taro. Several apple snails look alike, so shell color or a pink egg mass alone cannot settle the species identity.
identification: Photograph the shell, grooves, and egg mass without moving them. Expert examination may be needed to separate it from other introduced apple snails.
actions: Do not release aquarium snails or move snails, eggs, or contaminated plants between sites. Ask local aquatic or agricultural authorities about suspected populations.
researchNotes: EPPO supports current diagnosis and biology; the Hawaii chapter provides independent agricultural observations. Older P. insularum/maculata confusion was not used to assign records or impacts.

sources.title: EPPO Global Database: Pomacea canaliculata datasheet
Levin and colleagues: Apple snails in Hawaii

evidence.independentSourceGroup: European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization
claims: Freshwater plant feeder; shell and egg morphology; identification limits among apple snails.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Levin et al. Hawaii research team
claims: Introductions associated with food production and major damage to Hawaiian wetland taro.

proposedDescription: Charlock mustard, also called wild mustard, is an annual plant with clusters of bright yellow, four-petaled flowers. It often grows in cultivated fields and other disturbed ground, where its broad leaves and upright stems compete with crops for space and resources. Long seed pods follow the flowers, and seeds left in the soil can supply later generations. It belongs to the same plant family as many familiar vegetables, so recognizing its leaves, flowers, and pods together is more reliable than identifying it by color alone.
identification: Look for four yellow petals, rough or hairy foliage, and elongated pods. Other yellow-flowered mustards can be very similar.
actions: Remove unwanted plants before mature pods release seed. In crop fields, use local weed-management advice and monitor for later seedlings.
researchNotes: Cornell's weed account and NC State's botanical profile support an agricultural-weed description. Persistence is discussed without assigning a universal seed-longevity figure or legal status.

claims: Annual crop weed; seed persistence; management before seed return.
Yellow four-petaled flowers, hairy foliage and seed pods in disturbed habitats.

proposedDescription: The charru mussel is a small, thin-shelled mussel found in estuaries, lagoons, and other sheltered coastal waters. Its shell can range from greenish to nearly black, with a purple inner surface. It filters suspended food from the water and can gather on shells, roots, docks, and aquaculture structures. Introduced populations have become locally abundant, but abundance alone does not measure their effects: field research has found that competition with other mussels needs more careful study than some broad claims suggest.
identification: Look for a relatively smooth, thin shell with a purple interior. Native and other introduced mussels require expert comparison.
actions: Photograph suspect mussels in place and report unfamiliar fouling to local marine-resource staff. Avoid moving live mussels or fouled equipment between waters.
researchNotes: Smithsonian supports morphology and ecology; the independent 2023 Thailand survey, published in 2024, supports dense populations while cautioning about unproven displacement. M. charruana is an older name used in sources.

sources.title: Wells and colleagues: Charru mussel in the upper Gulf of Thailand

claims: Shell characters; estuarine habitat; suspension feeding and attached-substrate records.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Wells et al. Thailand field survey team
claims: Dense estuary and aquaculture populations; limited measured spread; uncertain competitive displacement.

proposedDescription: Chayote is a vigorous climbing vine best known for its pale-green, pear-shaped vegetable, also called mirliton or vegetable pear. The fruit contains a single large seed, and the vine uses supports to lift its cucumber-like leaves and developing crop above the ground. Separate male and female flowers grow on the same plant and attract pollinators. This tropical American crop is cultivated in warm regions around the world. Its presence in a garden is therefore different from a vine growing independently beyond cultivation.
identification: Look for a climbing cucurbit with cucumber-like leaves and a ridged or sometimes prickly, pear-shaped fruit containing one seed.
actions: Keep cultivated vines on suitable supports and within the growing area. Document escaped growth separately from deliberately planted crops.
researchNotes: UF/IFAS and the Indian Institute of Science support morphology and cultivation. Retained the queue's Sechium name; Sicyos edulis is noted in the flora as its basionym. No US ecological harm assumed.

sources.title: Indian Institute of Science: Sechium edule

claims: Climbing crop; separate male and female flowers; pear-shaped single-seeded fruit.
Perennial climber; hairy leaves, greenish flowers and cultivated edible fruit.

proposedDescription: Cheatgrass is an annual grass that often starts growing in fall, spends winter as a small plant, and produces seed early the following season. Its soft, hairy leaves give way to drooping, bristly seed heads, then dry vegetation as the season warms. In many western landscapes, this early-drying growth adds fine fuel between larger plants and can help fires spread. Repeated disturbance can favor more cheatgrass, making prevention of seed production and recovery of perennial vegetation important parts of long-term management.
identification: Look for soft hairs on the leaves and sheaths, a prominent membranous ligule, and nodding seed heads with long awns.
actions: Clean seeds from boots and equipment. For established patches, plan control before seed maturity and pair it with recovery of suitable perennial cover.
researchNotes: Illinois identification and Montana management accounts independently support the draft. Fire effects are framed for affected western landscapes, not every occurrence.

sources.title: Montana State Extension: Cheatgrass identification, biology and integrated management

claims: Hairy annual grass; drooping awned heads; early drying and western fire concern.
Seasonal life cycle; integrated control before seed production and perennial vegetation recovery.
